extracted.intended_audience: secondary/high-school mathematics teachers and mathematics educators (curriculum designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and materials for teaching mathematical problem solving in secondary/high-school classrooms using a 'Mathematics Practical' paradigm built on Pólya's four stages, Schoenfeld's framework, explicit scaffolding, and an associated assessment rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya's four-stage model
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the Problem; Devise a Plan; Carry out the Plan; Check and Expand — a hierarchical flowchart with allowed back-flow used as the core model for individual problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain each stage explicitly to students; use the model as a reference when stuck; allow loopbacks between stages; design worksheet pages so each page corresponds to a Pólya stage; encourage students to cycle through stages and to articulate which stage they are in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schoenfeld's framework (Resources, Heuristics, Control, Beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four aspects that contribute to success in problem solving: (1) Cognitive resources (facts/procedures), (2) Heuristics (rules of thumb), (3) Control (metacognitive regulation/efficiency), (4) Belief systems (attitudes about mathematics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the framework to diagnose student difficulties (e.g., lack of content knowledge vs. poor control); design instruction to develop resources, heuristics, control, and positive beliefs together rather than teaching heuristics alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage and assess the application of heuristics as central tools for exploring and planning solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristics listed and to be taught/used include: restate the problem in another way; work backwards; aim for sub-goals; divide into cases; use suitable numbers (instead of algebra); consider a simpler problem (smaller numbers, special cases, fewer variables); consider a more general case (loosen conditions); act it out; guess-and-check; make a systematic list; make a table; look for patterns; use equations/algebra; draw a diagram; use a suitable representation and notation. Use heuristics across Pólya stages (explore, devise, carry out).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Five criteria problems selected for instruction should satisfy: accessibility, multiplicity of solution paths, illustration of important ideas, constructibility (no tricks), and extendability/generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: (1) problems should be accessible to a wide range of students without heavy machinery/vocabulary; (2) solvable or approachable in more than one way to show richness; (3) illustrate important mathematical content or strategies; (4) be constructible/solvable without trickery; (5) serve as first steps for further exploration (extendable/generalizable). Use these when selecting tasks for Mathematics Practical lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics Practical lesson & worksheet design
rubrics_metrics.description: A 55-minute 'Mathematics Practical' lesson focused on one problem using a 4-page Practical Worksheet, each page corresponding to one Pólya stage, with permitted jump-to-stage options to differentiate students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow students who solve the problem quickly to jump to Stage 4 (Check and Expand) while requiring less-successful students to work through all four stages; allot up to 15 minutes for initial attempt (Stage 3); attach working-on-blank paper when necessary; design worksheet prompts to scaffold Pólya stages and promote metacognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaffolding levels for teacher help (Level 0, 1, 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three hierarchical levels of teacher assistance: Level 0 emphasizes Pólya stages and control (metacognitive prompting); Level 1 suggests specific heuristics; Level 2 gives problem-specific hints and should be avoided unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always begin with Level 0: ask 'What Pólya stage are you in?', 'Do you understand the problem?', 'What exactly are you doing?', 'Why are you doing that?'. If Level 0 fails, move to Level 1: suggest heuristics like 'try fewer lockers' or 'look for a pattern'. Use Level 2 only to protect student self-esteem and time (provides direct, problem-specific hints). The goal is for students to internalize Level 0 and rely minimally on Level 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment rubric for Practical Worksheet (20 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoring instrument focused on problem-solving processes with a total of 20 marks divided among main components: Polya's Stages [0–7], Heuristics [0–7], Checking and Expanding [0–6].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric encourages use of Pólya stages, application of heuristics, exhibition of control, and checking/extension. The design allows students to earn up to ~70% of marks for producing a correct solution (emphasizing process even when solution is absent) and requires Checking & Expanding work to reach distinction-level scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking and Expanding (assessment sub-criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Checking and Expanding criterion (total 0–6) further divided into: Providing alternative solutions [2], Evidence of checking correctness [1], Adapting/extending/generalizing the problem [3].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full marks for adapting/extending require either (a) two or more generalizations of the problem with solutions/suggestions, or (b) one significant extension with comments on solvability. Emphasize checking correctness and proposing alternative solutions as explicit assessed behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit control (metacognition) during problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should demonstrate metacognitive control: monitoring progress, choosing/justifying representations, pacing effort, deciding when to stop/store a problem, and iterating plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes explicit statements of stage, rationale for chosen representations (e.g., table, diagram, slash/cross notation), willingness to try modest goals before full-scale attack, use of control questions, and returning to earlier stages upon failure. Control is an assessed component in the rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize development of cognitive resources (content knowledge & representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure students have the necessary mathematical knowledge and fluent techniques (e.g., understanding 'multiples' and 'factors', prime factorization, efficient algebra) because weak resources impede any plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In planning curriculum and tasks, provide sufficient content support; teach and model useful representations (tables, diagrams, slash/cross notation) and notation that make carrying out plans feasible and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage extension, adaptation and generalization after solving
rubrics_metrics.description: After solving, students should 'Check and Expand' by finding more elegant/ general solutions, posing related problems (adaptations, extensions, converses), and exploring broader generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer scaffolded prompts and rubric credit for at least one significant extension or multiple generalizations; use posed adaptations (e.g., change which student reverses which lockers) as class exercises to reinforce methods and deepen understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment philosophy: assess process as well as product
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should drive instruction by valuing the problem-solving process (Pólya stages, heuristics, control, checking/expanding) alongside correct final answers, so that students study the process and not only solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rubrics and grading so that students can earn substantial marks for demonstrating process even if the final solution is incorrect; reserve top distinctions for demonstrable checking/extension work to incentivize deeper engagement.
